Charlotte Corday. Born in 1768, this noblewoman came from the Corday d'Armont family, minor Norman nobility with sympathies for the moderate Girondin faction. She had idealized the revolution's early, moderate phase, before it became radical and violent. In July 1793, she traveled to Paris with one deliberate purpose: to assassinate Jean-Paul Marat, the radical journalist she saw as the embodiment of revolutionary violence and the architect of the Girondins' destruction. She posed as a petitioner with information about royalist conspiracies to gain entry to Marat's home, and on July 13, 1793, she stabbed him in his medicinal bath. She made no attempt to escape and was arrested immediately. Tried within days of her act, she maintained her composure and conviction throughout the trial, arguing that she had killed a tyrant and a threat to true liberty. This composure earned admiration even from some revolutionaries. But her act backfired catastrophically. She was executed by guillotine on July 17, 1793, just four days after she stabbed Marat. Far from saving the revolution from extremism, her assassination made Marat a revolutionary icon and martyr. The revolutionaries used her act as justification for intensified persecution of suspected royalists and counter-revolutionaries, accelerating precisely the terror she had hoped to stop.
